chapter.title: Regularization, Bias and Variance
chapter.description: Bias/variance diagnosis, L2, L1, dropout, lab

questions.q: High variance means the model underfits the training set.
questions.explain: High bias = underfitting (the model does not even learn the training set). High variance = overfitting (good on train, poor generalization to dev/test).

questions.q: A train error of 18% and a dev error of 19% always means the model has high bias.
questions.explain: It depends on the human-level (optimal) error. If it is 0%, avoidable bias is 18% (high bias). If it is 16%, avoidable bias is only 2% and the model is good.

questions.q: The train error tells us about bias, and the gap between dev error and train error tells us about variance.
questions.explain: Bias is judged on the train set. Variance = dev error - train error.

questions.q: In L2 regularization, the bias vectors b are penalized together with the weights W.
questions.explain: Only W appears in the penalty. W has many entries while b has few, so penalizing b would change little. In the lab code, nothing is added for b1, b2, b3.

questions.q: Dividing the L2 penalty by m makes it weaker when we have more training data.
questions.explain: With the same weights, the penalty is 100 times smaller with 100 times more data. This is logical because more data already protects against overfitting.

questions.q: L2 regularization is called weight decay because, at every update, W is first multiplied by a factor (1 - αλ/m) smaller than 1.
questions.explain: W := (1 - αλ/m) W - α dW_data. The shrink factor is slightly below 1, so the weights decay at each step.

questions.q: L2 tends to push some weights to exactly 0, while L1 shrinks all weights smoothly.
questions.explain: It is the opposite. L1 (absolute values) tends to give sparse weights with some exactly 0. L2 (squares) shrinks all weights smoothly.

questions.q: Dropout is applied again at test time, so that predictions are averaged over many random sub-networks.
questions.explain: No dropout at test time: all neurons are used. This works thanks to the division by keep_prob during training, which keeps the expected activation the same.

questions.q: In inverted dropout, dividing the surviving activations by keep_prob keeps their expected value unchanged.
questions.explain: Shutting down neurons would reduce z of the next layer. Dividing by keep_prob compensates for it on average.

questions.q: Inside a layer, dropout shuts down the neurons that have the highest complexity.
questions.explain: The neurons are chosen randomly through the mask d. The only 'smart' choice is the keep_prob per layer, which can be lower for more complex layers.

questions.q: Regularization typically lowers the training accuracy but should improve the test accuracy.
questions.explain: It limits the ability of the network to memorize the training set, so train accuracy drops a bit while generalization improves.

questions.q: Dropout is normally applied to the output layer of the network.
questions.explain: It is applied to hidden layers. In the lab, layers 1 and 2 use dropout and the output layer does not.

questions.q: If λ is too large, the weights are squeezed toward 0 and the model underfits.
questions.explain: A boundary that is too simple gives high bias, with both train and test accuracy dropping. Too small a λ gives overfitting instead.

questions.q: In the lab, calling np.random.seed(1) inside forward_propagation_with_dropout gives the same masks at every iteration, unlike real dropout.
questions.explain: Real dropout draws new random masks at each iteration. Resetting the seed at every call can make the results behave differently from theory.

questions.q: Human-level error is 0%. Train error is 0.5% and dev error is 10%. What is the diagnosis?
options: High bias
High variance
High bias and high variance
Low bias and low variance
questions.explain: Bias is about 0.5%, which is fine. The gap between train and dev is 9.5%, so the model overfits (high variance).

questions.q: Human-level error is 16%. Train error is 18% and dev error is 19%. What is the diagnosis?
options: High bias
High variance
High bias and high variance
Low bias and low variance
questions.explain: Avoidable bias = 18 - 16 = 2% and variance = 19 - 18 = 1%. Both are small. With a human-level error of 0%, the same numbers would mean high bias.

questions.q: Human-level error is 16%. Train error is 30% and dev error is 45%. What is the diagnosis?
options: High variance only
High bias only
Both high bias and high variance
Neither
questions.explain: Avoidable bias = 14% and variance = 15%, so both problems are present.

questions.q: The train error is far above the acceptable error. What should you do first?
options: Increase λ
Add dropout
Collect more dev data
Use a bigger network or train longer
questions.explain: Bias is checked first: increase flexibility. Regularization (increase λ, dropout) is the remedy for high variance, and would make a high bias problem worse.

questions.q: Which expression is the L2-regularized cost of a neural network?
options: (1/m) Σ L + (λ/2m) Σ ||W[l]||F²
(1/m) Σ L + λ Σ |W[l]|
(1/m) Σ L - (λ/2m) Σ ||W[l]||F²
questions.explain: The penalty is the sum of the squares of all entries of every W (squared Frobenius norm) times λ/2m. B is the L1 shape, C penalizes b which is not done, and D has the wrong sign.

questions.q: With L2 regularization, what is dW[l]?
options: (1/m) dZ[l] A[l-1]ᵀ
(1/m) dZ[l] A[l-1]ᵀ - (λ/m) W[l]
(1/m) dZ[l] A[l-1]ᵀ + (λ/m) W[l]
(1/m) dZ[l] A[l-1]ᵀ + λ W[l]²
questions.explain: The derivative of (λ/2m) W² with respect to W is (λ/m) W, added to the usual gradient. A minus sign would make the weights grow.

questions.q: W = 3, m = 100, λ = 0.7, α = 0.3 and the data gradient is 0.05. What is W after one update with L2?
questions.explain: Penalty gradient = (0.7/100) × 3 = 0.021. Total gradient = 0.071. New W = 3 - 0.3 × 0.071 = 2.9787. Without L2 we would get 2.985.

questions.q: W = [2, -2, 1], m = 50, λ = 1. What is the L2 penalty (λ/2m) ||W||²?
questions.explain: ||W||² = 4 + 4 + 1 = 9, so the penalty is 9 / (2 × 50) = 0.09. Forgetting the 2 gives 0.18.

questions.q: Inverted dropout with keep_prob = 0.8 is applied to a = [5, 10, 15, 20] with mask [1, 1, 0, 1]. What is the result?
questions.explain: Apply the mask: [5, 10, 0, 20]. Then divide by 0.8: [6.25, 12.5, 0, 25]. Option A forgets the rescaling.

questions.q: What is the correct step for dA[l] in backpropagation with dropout?
options: dA = dA × keep_prob
dA = dA with no change
dA = dA ⊙ D / keep_prob, using the same mask as in the forward pass
dA = dA ⊙ (1 - D) / keep_prob
questions.explain: A neuron shut down in the forward pass contributed nothing, so it gets no gradient (same mask). The survivors were scaled by 1/keep_prob, so the gradient is scaled the same way.

questions.q: Why does a smaller W give a simpler model when the activation is tanh?
options: Because z stays small, where tanh is almost linear, so the network behaves like a linear model
Because tanh outputs become exactly 0
Because the number of neurons decreases
Because the learning rate is increased
questions.explain: For small z, tanh is almost a straight line. If every layer is nearly linear, the whole network is nearly linear, so it cannot make wild wiggles. No neuron is removed.

questions.q: What does keep_prob = 0.86 mean in the lab?
options: 86% of the neurons are shut down
Each neuron of the hidden layers is kept with probability 0.86 and shut down with probability 14%
The learning rate is multiplied by 0.86
The output layer is kept with probability 0.86 at test time
questions.explain: keep_prob is the probability of keeping a neuron. Option A reverses the meaning.

questions.q: Which statements about diagnosing bias and variance are correct? (select all)
options: The train error tells us about bias
The gap between dev error and train error tells us about variance
The human-level error is the reference used to judge what a good error is
The dev error alone is enough to diagnose the problem
questions.explain: The dev error alone cannot say whether the problem is bias or variance. We need the train error and the human-level reference.

questions.q: Which actions help against high variance? (select all)
options: Add neurons to the layers
L2 regularization
Dropout
Get more training data
questions.explain: Adding neurons increases flexibility, which is a remedy for high bias and would worsen overfitting.

questions.q: Which statements about λ are correct? (select all)
options: Too low a value leads to overfitting (high variance)
Too high a value leads to underfitting (high bias)
It is a hyperparameter tuned on the dev set
It is learned by gradient descent like W
questions.explain: λ is chosen by us, not learned. W and b are the learned parameters.

questions.q: Which statements about dropout are correct? (select all)
options: It is used only during training
Activations are divided by keep_prob after applying the mask
The same mask is reused in backpropagation
At test time, neurons are dropped with probability 1 - keep_prob
questions.explain: At test time all neurons are used, with no dropout.

questions.q: Why does dropout reduce overfitting? (select all)
options: At each iteration the network is smaller, so less complex
No neuron is essential, so the decision is spread over many units
The network cannot rely on specific neurons
It increases the number of parameters to learn
questions.explain: Dropout does not add parameters. It reduces the reliance on specific units.

questions.q: Which statements about L1 and L2 are correct? (select all)
options: L1 penalizes the absolute values of the weights
L2 penalizes the squares of the weights
L2 pushes many weights to exactly 0
L1 tends to give sparse weights
questions.explain: Exactly-zero weights are typical of L1. L2 shrinks all weights smoothly. The lab uses L2.

questions.q: Why is the L2 penalty divided by m? (select all)
options: It stays on the same scale as the averaged loss
It fades as the amount of data grows
It keeps λ comparable across datasets of different sizes
It makes the biases regularized as well
questions.explain: The division by m has nothing to do with the biases, which are not penalized.

questions.q: Which expectations about the lab experiments are correct? (select all)
options: Regularization may lower the train accuracy
Test accuracy should improve compared with the baseline
With a very large λ the boundary can be over-smoothed (high bias)
The model works only if both lambd and keep_prob are non-zero
questions.explain: The function asserts lambd == 0 or keep_prob == 1: one technique at a time.

questions.q: Define bias and variance using N models trained on N different training sets from the same distribution.
questions.answer: Bias: how far the predictions are from the true values on average (the models are consistently wrong, low accuracy): underfitting. Variance: how much the performance changes from one model to another (the accuracies on a validation set are dispersed), because each model became specific to its own training set, including its outliers: overfitting.
questions.explain: High bias = underfitting, high variance = overfitting. Do not reverse them.

questions.q: How do you diagnose a model using the human-level error? Compare train 18% / dev 19% for a human-level error of 0% and of 16%.
questions.answer: Avoidable bias = train error - human-level error, and variance = dev error - train error. With 0%: avoidable bias 18%, so high bias. With 16%: avoidable bias 2% and variance 1%, so low bias and low variance. The same numbers give a different verdict.
questions.explain: Always give the reference before judging.

questions.q: What is the methodology to improve a deep network, and in which order?
questions.answer: 1) Check the train performance: if bias is high, increase flexibility (more layers or neurons, train longer) and repeat. 2) Then check the dev performance: if variance is high, use regularization (L2, dropout) and, if possible, more data. Bias first, then variance, and we do not go back once bias is fixed.
questions.explain: Training is an iterative loop: Idea, Code, Experiment.

questions.q: Write the L2-regularized cost of a neural network and define each symbol.
questions.answer: J = (1/m) Σ L(ŷ(i), y(i)) + (λ/2m) Σ_l ||W[l]||F². m is the number of training examples, L the loss of one example, λ the regularization hyperparameter, and ||W[l]||F² the sum of the squares of all entries of W[l]. Biases are not penalized.
questions.explain: The first term fits the data, the second keeps the weights small.

questions.q: Show that L2 regularization makes the weights decrease.
questions.answer: The penalty adds (λ/m) W to dW, so W := W - α(dW_data + (λ/m) W) = (1 - αλ/m) W - α dW_data. Since 1 - αλ/m is smaller than 1 (and positive), W is multiplied by a factor below 1 at every step: weight decay.
questions.explain: Mention the condition 1 - αλ/m > 0, otherwise the weight would change sign at each step.

questions.q: Why is the penalty (λ/2m) and not just λ?
questions.answer: Dividing by m puts the penalty on the same scale as the averaged loss and makes it fade as the data grows, since more data already reduces overfitting. The factor 1/2 cancels the 2 coming from the derivative of W², giving a gradient of exactly (λ/m) W.
questions.explain: Example: with ||W||² = 10 and λ = 0.7, the penalty is 0.35 for m = 10 but 0.0035 for m = 1000.

questions.q: What is the effect of a very small and of a very large λ?
questions.answer: Too small (or 0): little constraint, complex wiggly boundary, overfitting (high variance). Too large: the weights are squeezed toward 0, the boundary is too simple and over-smoothed, underfitting (high bias) with train and test accuracy both dropping. A right value gives a smooth boundary and the best test accuracy.
questions.explain: λ is tuned on the dev set.

questions.q: Explain inverted dropout: the steps, why we divide by keep_prob, and what happens at test time.
questions.answer: For each hidden layer, build a random mask D (1 with probability keep_prob, else 0), compute A = A × D to shut neurons down, then A = A / keep_prob. The division keeps the expected value of the activations unchanged, since shutting neurons down would reduce the next z. At test time nothing is dropped: all neurons are used, and no correction is needed.
questions.explain: In backpropagation, reuse the same mask and divide by keep_prob too.

questions.q: Why does dropout reduce overfitting, and how can keep_prob be chosen?
questions.answer: At each iteration the network is smaller (less complexity) and no neuron is essential, so the decision is spread out instead of relying on specific units. keep_prob is a hyperparameter that can differ per layer: lower values for the more complex layers, and almost never dropout on the input layer. Use dropout only when facing overfitting.
questions.explain: It is very successful in computer vision.

questions.q: To decide whether a train error of 18% and a dev error of 19% is good, we need the human-level error as a reference.
questions.explain: The human-level (optimal) error defines what a good error is, and gives the avoidable bias.

questions.q: With L2 regularization, dW[l] gets an additional term (λ/m) W[l], while db[l] is unchanged.
questions.explain: Only W is penalized. The derivative of (λ/2m) ||W||² is (λ/m) W.

questions.q: Dropout should be switched on by default for every network.
questions.explain: Use dropout only when facing overfitting. It is not a default switch.

questions.q: Human-level error is 1%. Train error is 2% and dev error is 12%. What is the best next step?
options: Use a bigger network
Train for longer
Add regularization (L2 or dropout) or collect more data
Do nothing, the model is good
questions.explain: Avoidable bias is about 1% (fine) and variance is 10%, so the problem is high variance. Bigger networks and longer training are for high bias.

questions.q: In the lab, α = 0.3, λ = 0.7 and m = 211. What is the shrink factor 1 - αλ/m applied to each weight?
options: About 0.999
questions.explain: αλ/m = 0.21 / 211 ≈ 0.001, so the factor is about 0.999: tiny per step, but strong over 30,000 iterations.

questions.q: What happens to dropout at test time?
options: The mask is drawn with keep_prob = 0.5
Dropout is not applied: all neurons are used
Only the output layer is kept
Half of the weights are set to 0
questions.explain: No dropout at test time. The division by keep_prob during training already makes the expected values match.

questions.q: Train error 15%, dev error 16%, human-level error 1%. Which statements are correct? (select all)
options: Avoidable bias is 14%
Variance is only 1%
The first action should be to increase the flexibility of the model
Adding dropout is the right first action
questions.explain: The problem is high bias (underfitting). Regularization is for high variance and would not help.

questions.q: Which statements about dropout backpropagation are correct? (select all)
options: A neuron shut down in the forward pass receives no gradient
The same mask as in the forward pass is used
dA is divided by keep_prob
The masks are generated again, independently from the forward pass
questions.explain: The masks are saved in the cache during the forward pass and reused.

questions.q: W = [2, -2, 1], m = 50, λ = 1, α = 0.5. Compute the L2 penalty, the gradient contribution (λ/m) W, and the update of W assuming a zero data gradient.
questions.explain: The update shows weight decay clearly: every weight shrinks by 1%.

questions.q: Apply inverted dropout with keep_prob = 0.8 to a = [5, 10, 15, 20] with mask [1, 1, 0, 1]. Explain why the rescaling is needed.
questions.answer: After the mask: [5, 10, 0, 20]. After dividing by 0.8: [6.25, 12.5, 0, 25]. The rescaling keeps the expected activation equal to its value without dropout, so the next layer's z is not reduced and no correction is needed at test time.
questions.explain: One random sample can differ from the no-dropout value, but the average over many masks matches it.

questions.q: Regularization lowered the training accuracy of your network. Is that a problem?
questions.answer: No. Regularization limits the ability of the network to memorize the training set, so train accuracy drops a bit, but test accuracy should improve. A model is judged on its generalization (test) performance, not on its training accuracy.
questions.explain: If both train and test drop a lot, λ may be too large (underfitting).
